candidate_relations.reason: A large symptomatic periprosthetic soft-tissue mass and markedly elevated alkaline phosphatase establish that a substantive pathologic process is present.
Mild CRP elevation and an aspirate white-cell count of 10,750 per microliter can reflect inflammation around the mass but do not identify the osteogenic malignancy.
The implant was ceramic-on-ceramic and serum cobalt and chromium were normal, making a metal-on-metal ALTR an alternative rather than the final osteosarcoma diagnosis.
The elevated aspirate cell count raised infection as a consideration, but all cultures were negative and a 9-by-8-by-10-centimeter mass remained unexplained.
Eleven years after arthroplasty the presentation could mimic chronic infection, yet repeated culture evidence in the provided aspiration was negative and systemic infectious symptoms were absent.
The patient denied fever and cultures from hip aspiration were all negative, so chronic periprosthetic hip infection does not equal the referenced tumor.
A ceramic-on-ceramic articulation with normal cobalt and chromium levels does not support metal-debris disease as the identity of the large mass.
Periprosthetic infection was clinically plausible from pain and aspirate leukocytosis, but negative cultures and no systemic symptoms distinguish it from the final osteosarcoma.
The record's mass could prompt a neoplastic differential, but lymphoma is a distinct tumor lineage from the referenced osteogenic sarcoma and no lymphoid evidence is reported.
Normal serum metal-ion levels and a ceramic bearing provide no record support for metallosis as the explanation for the periprosthetic mass.
Osteogenic sarcoma is a standard synonym for osteosarcoma, consistent with the painful large mass and markedly elevated alkaline phosphatase in this case.
MRI explicitly showed no bony involvement or marrow edema, so osteolysis neither matches the imaging nor names the referenced sarcoma.
The lesion was confined to periprosthetic soft tissue without bone involvement, which argues against periprosthetic osteolysis as the final object.
An adverse local tissue reaction can produce a periprosthetic mass, but the ceramic articulation and normal metal levels do not establish it and it is not the referenced malignancy.
